451.quote_or_event: “When reprimanded a wise man should not be angry, but he should be of a forbearing mood; he should not associate, laugh, and play with mean men.”
451.explanation: In the opening lecture on discipline, the well-trained disciple is told plainly to keep away from the company and pastimes of mean men.
451.tie_back: Valluvar says greatness shrinks from the company of the mean-minded. Here the Jain disciple's discipline likewise includes refusing to keep company with such people.
451.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
451._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Direct match on avoiding mean company. The Kural's contrast with small minds gathering such people as kin is not present.

452.quote_or_event: “Water when mixed with milk will become milk, not remaining water. Will it exhibit the appearance of water? In like manner, if you consider it, the meanness of the mean when united with the dignity of the excellent will utterly vanish.”
452.explanation: The Naladiyar uses the image of water taking on the nature of the milk it is mixed with to show that a person takes on the character of the company they join.
452.tie_back: This is the same liquid image as the kural, where water changes with the soil it runs through and the mind changes with its company. Here it is shown from the hopeful side, as the mean are transformed by the excellent.
452.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 7 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
452._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Very close in image and argument, but from a Tamil Jain didactic text rather than canonical scripture.

453.quote_or_event: “Though innocent in intention, persons will be despised on account of the (bad) company they have joined. In the forest both the scent-giving sandal and the teak tree will be burned when the brushwood, which has been cut, has caught fire.”
453.explanation: The Naladiyar warns that even a person with a pure inner intention is judged, and suffers, by the company they keep, just as fine sandalwood burns along with the brushwood around it.
453.tie_back: Valluvar sets inner perception, which comes from the mind, against the verdict 'he is such a man', which comes from one's company. The Naladiyar makes the same split between innocent intention and reputation earned through company.
453.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
453._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Near one-to-one on reputation coming from company despite inner intention. It is a Tamil Jain text, not canonical scripture.

454.quote_or_event: “When the worthy teachers, who are thoroughly enlightened and from early times well versed in conduct, are satisfied (with a pupil), they will make over to him their extensive and weighty knowledge of the sacred texts.”
454.explanation: In Jain monastic life, knowledge of the scriptures passes from teacher to pupil; a disciple's learning is literally handed over by the enlightened company he serves.
454.tie_back: The kural holds that wisdom seems to live in one's own mind but really lives in one's company. The Jain verse likewise has the pupil's wisdom come from the worthy teachers whose company he has won.
454.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.46 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
454._accuracy_note: Checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote markers removed). Reasonable fit on knowledge coming from one's company, but it does not share the Kural's claim that wisdom only appears to belong to one's own mind.

455.quote_or_event: “Living in this (company of the teacher) and protecting (himself or other beings) in the three ways (viz. in thoughts, words, and acts), he (gets) peace and the annihilation (of sins) as they say.”
455.explanation: The Sutrakritanga ties the purification of thought, word and deed, and the destruction of sin, to the monk's staying in the company of his teacher.
455.tie_back: Valluvar says purity of mind and of deeds both come through purity of company. In the Jain verse, too, guarding thought, word and act and wearing away sin happen within that good company.
455._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Good match on purity of mind and deed through company, though Jacobi's bracketed glosses show that the reading depends partly on the commentators.

456.quote_or_event: “He who adopts the conduct which the wise ones have attained by their virtues and always practised, will not incur blame.”
456.explanation: The lecture on discipline promises that one who takes on the conduct practised by the wise will do nothing that deserves blame.
456.tie_back: The kural's second line says those whose company is pure do no deed that is not good. The Jain verse likewise says that following the wise keeps one free of blameworthy acts.
456.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.42 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
456._accuracy_note: Checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed). It matches only the kural's second line. Nothing here corresponds to the first line on the good legacy (eccham) of the pure-minded.

457.quote_or_event: “Even the hare in the wide, beauteous, and sublime heavens, since it is seen in the moon with refulgent beams, will be adored (by men). And in like manner even those who are without any dignity (of their own), if they obtain the love of the good, who are as mountains of virtue, will have dignity.”
457.explanation: The Naladiyar says that just as the hare seen on the moon is honoured because of the moon, people who have no standing of their own gain dignity through the affection of the good.
457.tie_back: Valluvar says goodness of company brings every kind of renown. The Naladiyar's hare in the moon shows good company conferring honour on someone who would otherwise have none.
457.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 6 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
457._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Strong fit on renown through company, but it does not have the Kural's pairing of a good mind with prosperity. It is a Tamil Jain text.

458.quote_or_event: “A Sramana engaged in austerities, who longs for righteousness, should eat the proper quantity of allowed food, should select a companion of right understanding, and should live in a place suited to seclusion.” … “If he does not meet with a clever companion who surpasses or equals him in virtue, he should live by himself, abstaining from sins and not devoted to pleasures.”
458.explanation: Even the ascetic already devoted to austerity and righteousness is told to choose a companion of right understanding, ideally one equal or superior in virtue. Jainism also allows him to live alone rather than accept a lesser companion.
458.tie_back: The kural says that even for the already virtuous, good company is a source of security. The Jain text likewise has even the advanced ascetic seek a worthy companion, though it qualifies the need more than Valluvar does.
458.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.4–5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
458._accuracy_note: Checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics in 'Sramana' simplified, footnote markers removed). The fit is partial: Jainism values solitude for the advanced monk (cf. 32.5 and 32.16), whereas the Kural treats good company as a support even for the wise.

459.quote_or_event: “His knowledge will be honoured, his doubts will be removed, he will gladden the heart of his teacher by his good acts; kept in safety by the performance of austerities and by meditation, being as it were a great light, he will keep the five vows.” … “Honoured by gods, Gandharvas, and men, he will, on leaving this body which consists of dirt and impurities, become either an eternal Siddha, or a god of great power and small imperfections.”
459.explanation: The lecture on discipline ends by following the disciple who has served his teachers beyond death, to rebirth as a powerful god or to final liberation as a Siddha.
459.tie_back: Valluvar says bliss in the world to come is earned by goodness of mind and made secure by good company. The Jain disciple's reward after death likewise comes through his own vows and his bond with his teachers.
459.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.47–48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
459._accuracy_note: Checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed). Both texts link good company to the next life, but in Jainism the highest goal is liberation (siddhahood), which goes beyond a heavenly reward.

460.quote_or_event: “Like paddy multiplied through the goodness of the soil, persons will become good through the goodness of their respective families. Like the destruction of a good ship on the approach of a strong gale, goodness will be destroyed by bad company.”
460.explanation: The Naladiyar sets the growth of goodness through a good setting against the way bad company wrecks goodness, like a ship broken by a gale.
460.tie_back: This mirrors the closing superlative of the kural, where nothing helps more than good company and nothing harms more than bad. The Naladiyar sets the same two outcomes side by side.
460.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 9 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
460._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Strong two-sided fit. The first half speaks of family (kudi) rather than company, and this is a Tamil Jain text rather than canonical scripture.
